t: Triples with Bitwise AND Equal To Zero — Editorial
o: We must count ordered index triples (i, j, k) whose bitwise AND is zero. In Example 1 ([2,1,3]) only triples where at least one element contributes a bit the others lack give AND = 0; e.g. any triple containing both a 1 (bit 0) and a 2 (bit 1) works, giving 12. In Example 2 all elements are 0, so every one of the 3^3 = 27 ordered triples qualifies. With n up to 1000, an O(n^3) brute force does ~10^9 operations — too slow in practice, so we need to precompute something about pairs. Since values are < 2^16, there are only 65536 possible masks, which makes counting by mask value very attractive.
k: The answer counts ordered triples, so pair counts can be reused directly without dividing.
There are at most 2^16 distinct values, so we can bucket numbers by their bitmask.
Meet in the middle: count pairs (i, j) by their AND result, then for each k count masks that are supersets of nums[k] via subset-sum (SOS) DP.

a.i: Directly check every ordered triple (i, j, k) and increment the answer when nums[i] & nums[j] & nums[k] == 0. This is the most intuitive solution and matches the problem definition exactly, but with n = 1000 it performs about 10^9 AND operations, which is too slow for typical time limits yet fine for tiny inputs.
s: Loop i from 0 to n-1, j from 0 to n-1, k from 0 to n-1.
If nums[i] & nums[j] & nums[k] == 0, increment ans.
a.t: O(n^3) — three nested loops over all indices (~10^9 operations for n = 1000).

a.n: Approach 2: Count Pairs by Mask Value
a.i: Instead of iterating over pairs of indices, iterate over pairs of distinct values. Build cnt[v] = number of array elements equal to v (at most 2^16 values). Then for each pair of values (a, b), the pair AND a & b occurs cnt[a] * cnt[b] times among ordered index pairs. For each such pair-AND p, add cnt[p] * cnt[a] * cnt[b] to the answer, since a third element z satisfies p & z == 0 exactly when z equals some value whose AND with p is zero — checking each distinct z against p costs O(2^16) per distinct pair, but total distinct-value pairs are at most 2^32... so instead we cap work by noting only values present matter. A cleaner bound: loop over present values a, b (up to min(n, 2^16)^2 pairs) and for each pair-AND p add cnt[p] * (number of elements z with z & p == 0), computed by scanning all present values once per pair — O(V^3) worst case but V <= 1000 effectively when n limits distinct values, giving O(n^2 * V).
s: Build cnt[mask] = frequency of each value in nums.
Collect the list of distinct present values.
For each ordered pair of distinct values (a, b), compute p = a & b.
For each distinct value z with z & p == 0, add cnt[a] * cnt[b] * cnt[z] to the answer.
a.t: O(min(n, 2^16)^3) — triple loop over distinct values; with n = 1000 this is at most 10^9 but typically far less since duplicates collapse; still slower than Approach 3 in the worst case.

a.n: Approach 3: Pair Counting + Subset-Sum (SOS) DP — Optimal
a.i: Count freq[p] = number of ordered index pairs (i, j) with nums[i] & nums[j] = p, in O(n^2). Then the answer is sum over k of freq[p] where p & nums[k] == 0, i.e. p must be a submask of ~nums[k]. Using a subset-sum (SOS / zeta transform) over all 2^16 masks, sup[m] = number of pairs whose AND is a submask of m, computed in O(2^16 * 16). The answer is then sum over k of sup[~nums[k] & 0xFFFF]. This reduces the whole problem to roughly 10^6 + 10^6 operations.
s: Build freq[mask] for all 2^16 masks: for each ordered pair (i, j) increment freq[nums[i] & nums[j]].
Run SOS DP: for each bit b, for each mask m with bit b set, add freq[m ^ (1<<b)] into freq[m], so freq[m] becomes the count of pairs whose AND is a submask of m.
For each k, add freq[(~nums[k]) & 0xFFFF] to the answer.
a.t: O(n^2 + 2^16 * 16) — building the pair-frequency table dominates at ~10^6 operations; SOS DP adds ~10^6 more.

w: In an interview, start with brute force to show understanding, mention the duplicate-value optimization, then land on the SOS DP approach as the intended solution. Key pitfalls: forgetting triples are **ordered** (never divide by anything), mishandling the complement mask (use `(~x) & 0xFFFF` since Python ints are unbounded), and integer overflow in C++/Java (use 64-bit accumulation before casting). Edge cases: all zeros (answer n^3), single element 0 (answer 1), single nonzero element (answer 0). Likely follow-ups: what if values go up to 2^20 or larger (SOS still viable up to ~2^22), or if you needed unordered triples instead (inclusion–exclusion on multiplicities gets messy — discuss carefully).
